rows.title: Traditional Chinese Medicine as an Adjunct in Hyperthyroidism Management: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Proposed Mechanisms, and Clinical Evidence.
rows.verified_title: Traditional Chinese Medicine as an Adjunct in Hyperthyroidism Management: A Narrative Review of Pathophysiology, Proposed Mechanisms, and Clinical Evidence.
rows.focus: Hyperthyroidism, characterized by elevated serum thyroxine levels, can be classified into overt and subclinical forms. Untreated hyperthyroidism poses substantial health risks. Antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, and surgery are established conventional therapeutic options; however, their clinical application may be limited by relapse, adverse effects, contraindications, or patient preference. This narrative review examines the epidemiology of hyperthyroidism, particularly its association with iodine status, strong genetic predisposition, clinical manifestations predominantly seen in women of reproductive age, and diagnostic strategies. Pathophysiological mechanisms of different hyperthyroidism subtypes, including Graves' disease and thyrotoxicosis caused by hyperfunctioning thyroid nodules, are discussed in detail. Furthermore, the perspective of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) is explored, which attributes hyperthyroidism to Gan-Qi (liver-qi) disturbance and identifies exuberant liver fire as a core pathogenic factor. Multi-faceted mechanisms of TCM interventions, largely derived from network-pharmacology, pre-clinical findings and limited clinical data, represent proposed, hypothesis-generating pathways rather than firmly confirmed clinical effects. Available small-sized and heterogeneous randomized controlled trials suggest possible adjunctive benefits of TCM formulas and integrative therapies, such as Gardenia Qinggan Decoction combined with acupuncture, yet the overall certainty of evidence remains limited. Finally, this review highlights challenges in the standardization of TCM interventions, and underscores the necessity for unified quality-control metrics and standardized syndrome-differentiation criteria. Long-term comparative data evaluating sustained clinical outcomes of TCM-integrated management are still required.

rows.title: Cancer and the microbiome: from association to intervention.
rows.verified_title: Cancer and the microbiome: from association to intervention.
rows.focus: The gut microbiome is increasingly recognised as a clinically modifiable determinant of efficacy and toxicity across systemic cancer therapies, with the most mature evidence in patients receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). The composition and function of intestinal microbes can influence treatment outcomes by affecting immune priming, antigen presentation, host-microbial co-metabolism, drug biotransformation, and epithelial barrier integrity. In melanoma, non-small-cell lung cancer, and renal cell carcinoma, higher microbial diversity, ecological stability, and enrichment of immunostimulatory pathways have been associated with improved ICI response and survival. By contrast, antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors are linked to inferior outcomes because they disrupt the microbiome. Microbiome-directed interventions, including faecal microbiota transplantation, dietary modifications, prebiotics, probiotics, and live biotherapeutic products, are undergoing clinical testing but remain at the investigational stage. This Review synthesises current evidence linking the intestinal microbiome to anticancer therapy outcomes, evaluates strategies and challenges for therapeutic modulation of the microbiome, and introduces emerging insights into the mycobiome.

rows.title: Fucoidan as an anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agent in humans: a systematic review of clinical evidence and translational potential.
rows.verified_title: Fucoidan as an anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory agent in humans: a systematic review of clinical evidence and translational potential.
rows.focus: Purpose: fucoidan is a sulphated polysaccharide from brown seaweeds, commonly used as a dietary supplement due to its proposed anti-inflammatory, immunomodulatory, and potential tumour-related properties. However, despite substantial preclinical evidence, its clinical effects in humans remain unclear. This systematic review aims to evaluate and synthesise current clinical evidence on the effects of fucoidan on inflammatory, immune, metabolic, and tumour-related outcomes in humans. Methods: a systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science in accordance with the PRISMA guidelines. Human interventional studies evaluating fucoidan supplementation and reporting clinically relevant outcomes were included. Eligible populations comprised healthy adults, individuals with metabolic or inflammatory conditions, and patients with cancer. Outcomes included immune function, inflammatory biomarkers, metabolic parameters, tumour-related outcomes, quality of life, and safety. Risk of bias was assessed using the OHAT tool. Due to heterogeneity in study design and outcomes, meta-analysis was not performed. Results: five clinical studies met the inclusion criteria, including three randomised controlled trials and two open-label studies involving patients with cancer, with intervention durations of 2 to 24 weeks. Fucoidan was consistently well-tolerated, with no serious adverse events reported. Individual controlled trials reported reductions in selected pro-inflammatory cytokines, sex-specific changes in NK cell activity, and changes in gut microbiota composition in individuals with metabolic risk. However, these findings were not consistently replicated across studies. Studies involving patients with cancer reported short-term reductions in inflammatory markers and stable quality-of-life (QOL) measures; however, tumour-related outcomes were inconclusive. Conclusions: current evidence suggests that fucoidan may exert modest anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects under selected clinical conditions; however, the available evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and inconsistent. Although oral fucoidan was generally well tolerated, the small number of studies, limited replication of findings, heterogeneity in study populations and fucoidan characteristics, and methodological limitations preclude definitive conclusions regarding clinical efficacy. Well-designed, adequately powered randomised controlled trials using well-characterised fucoidan and clinically meaningful outcomes are required to establish the clinical efficacy of fucoidan in humans.

rows.title: Traditional Chinese medicine for Helicobacter pylori infection in the antibiotic-resistance era: Ethnopharmacological evidence, mechanisms, and Host-Pathogen modulation.
rows.verified_title: Traditional Chinese medicine for Helicobacter pylori infection in the antibiotic-resistance era: Ethnopharmacological evidence, mechanisms, and Host-Pathogen modulation.
rows.focus: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection remains a global health burden, and antibiotic resistance has reduced the effectiveness of standard eradication regimens. In traditional Chinese medicine (TCM), persistent infection is interpreted as retention of pathogenic factors in the spleen-stomach system. Herbal formulas are investigated as adjunctive strategies, but their clinical roles and mechanistic basis require clarification. To develop a host-pathogen modulation framework integrating clinical evidence, antibiotic resistance and persistence mechanisms, and TCM pharmacology, while distinguishing clinically supported effects from preclinical plausibility. This critical narrative review was based on a structured search of six databases from inception through April 2026. Evidence was synthesized without quantitative pooling. Some TCM formulas used with standard regimens were associated with improved eradication outcomes, whereas others showed similar eradication rates with possible advantages in symptom relief, tolerability, or adverse-event reduction. However, confidence in the clinical evidence remains low because most studies were small, single-center trials with heterogeneous interventions and comparators, incomplete risk-of-bias reporting, inconsistent outcome definitions, limited follow-up, and inadequate safety assessment. Preclinical studies suggest that formulas, herbs, and compounds may affect bacterial growth and colonization fitness, urease, adhesion, virulence systems, biofilm-associated tolerance, mucosal injury, inflammation, and gastric-gut microecology. Interpretation of these mechanisms is further limited by inconsistent quantitative pharmacological data, uncertain gastric exposure and pharmacokinetics, and weak linkage between experimental findings and clinical outcomes. TCM should not replace standard eradication therapy. Its more defensible role is as a potential host-pathogen modulatory strategy with adjunctive, supportive, and mucosa-protective value. The current clinical findings should be regarded as preliminary rather than confirmatory. Rigorous multicenter trials, standardized interventions, quantitative pharmacology, pharmacokinetic validation, and mechanism-linked clinical studies are required.

rows.title: Recent Studies on the Effectiveness and Safety of Anti-Obesity Medications: A Scoping Review.
rows.journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
rows.verified_title: Recent Studies on the Effectiveness and Safety of Anti-Obesity Medications: A Scoping Review.
rows.verified_journal: Diabetes, metabolic syndrome and obesity : targets and therapy
rows.focus: Obesity remains a major global public health challenge associated with increased morbidity, mortality, and reduced quality of life, necessitating effective treatment strategies beyond lifestyle modifications. The present scoping review aimed to synthesize recent evidence on the effectiveness and safety of anti-obesity medications (AOMs). A structured literature search was conducted in PubMed and Scopus in May 2025 to identify original studies published within the previous five years involving individuals with overweight or obesity receiving pharmacological interventions. A total of 42 articles representing 41 unique studies, predominantly randomized controlled trials (RCTs), were included in the evidence synthesis. The review encompassed glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RA), including semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide, and orforglipron; multi-receptor incretin agonists, including tirzepatide, retatrutide, and survodutide; amylin-based combination therapy (cagrilintide plus semaglutide); established non-incretin AOMs (orlistat, phentermine, phentermine/topiramate, and naltrexone/bupropion); microbiome-targeted therapies; and nutraceutical-based interventions. Among these, GLP-1 RA consistently demonstrated substantial weight-loss efficacy, with semaglutide achieving approximately 10-16% weight loss, while tirzepatide produced approximately 15-21% weight reduction over treatment durations of 20-70 weeks. Emerging multi-receptor incretin agonists also demonstrated promising efficacy, whereas established non-incretin AOMs, microbiome-targeted therapies, and nutraceutical-based interventions generally produced modest or more heterogeneous outcomes. Gastrointestinal adverse events (AEs) were the most frequently reported across incretin-based therapies. Overall, incretin-based therapies currently provide the greatest weight-loss benefit, although evidence for several emerging pharmacotherapies, microbiome-targeted therapies, and nutraceutical-based interventions remains limited. Further well-designed comparative trials, mechanistic studies, and long-term real-world investigations are needed to better establish the durability, safety, and clinical applicability of emerging AOMs.

rows.title: Harnessing Terminalia arjuna in Next Generation Phytomedicine: Cutting Edge Nutraceutical Trends Shaping Food and Health.
rows.verified_title: Harnessing Terminalia arjuna in Next Generation Phytomedicine: Cutting Edge Nutraceutical Trends Shaping Food and Health.
rows.focus: Phytomedicines are increasingly favored as alternatives to modern treatment due to their enhanced efficacy and cultural relevance in preserving traditional healing knowledge while supporting sustainable healthcare practices. Among them, Terminalia arjuna stands out as a widely consumed dietary and Ayurvedic remedy. This review explores the pharmacological evidence for T. arjuna and its relevance to food science and toxicology, unveiling its molecular mechanisms in health and disease. They target the axis of p53-PARP mediated apoptosis, endoplasmic reticulum stress mechanisms, mitochondrial integrity, and TGF-β mediated remodeling processes. T. arjuna's major bioactive constituents like arjunic acid, arjunolic acid, and casuarinin, to name a few, possess antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, cardioprotective, renal, and liver-protective capacities. In this work, we critically evaluate the strength of preclinical versus clinical evidence and identify the gaps in bioavailability, safety, and herb-drug interaction data, beyond its pharmacological profile, to establish T. arjuna's translational potential. This study further explores T. arjuna as a candidate for modern nutraceutical and functional food development while highlighting the need for future validations before its full potential is confirmed.

rows.title: Clinical efficacy of integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients with coronary artery disease.
rows.verified_title: Clinical efficacy of integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine in patients with coronary artery disease.
rows.focus: Coronary artery disease (CAD) remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Although guideline-directed Western medical therapy improves cardiovascular outcomes, residual symptoms remain common. Integrated traditional Chinese and Western medicine is frequently used as an adjunctive strategy in China, but its real-world, short-term clinical associations require further characterization. This retrospective observational study included 215 patients with CAD treated between January 2022 and December 2024, including 106 patients receiving conventional Western medical therapy alone and 109 receiving adjunctive traditional Chinese medicine based on syndrome differentiation. Symptom status, laboratory parameters, overall clinical response, and documented adverse events were compared between groups. Because treatment allocation was nonrandom and the analyses were unadjusted for potential confounders, all between-group findings were interpreted as associations. No statistically significant differences were observed in the measured baseline demographic, clinical, or laboratory characteristics between the 2 groups. After treatment, the integrated-treatment group had lower rates of residual chest pain, chest tightness, and fatigue and greater changes in total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, fibrinogen, and D-dimer. The observed overall clinical response rate was higher in the integrated-treatment group (90.8% vs 76.4%, P = .004). Documented adverse-event incidence did not differ significantly between groups. In this retrospective real-world cohort, adjunctive traditional Chinese medicine was associated with greater short-term improvement in selected symptoms and laboratory parameters and a higher observed clinical response rate, without a detectable increase in documented short-term adverse events. These unadjusted observational findings are exploratory, do not establish causal superiority or improved cardiovascular prognosis, and are insufficient by themselves to modify current guideline-directed CAD practice.

rows.title: From Identification to Enzymatic Activity Profiling: Comprehensive Characterization of BloCAβ, a Probiotic β-Carbonic Anhydrase From Bifidobacterium longum.
rows.verified_title: From Identification to Enzymatic Activity Profiling: Comprehensive Characterization of BloCAβ, a Probiotic β-Carbonic Anhydrase From Bifidobacterium longum.
rows.focus: The microbiota comprises communities of microorganisms that establish complex relationships with the host and play key roles in physiology, metabolism, and immunity. Increasing evidence highlights microbiota alterations in several diseases, particularly those driven by oxidative stress-induced inflammation. Thus, identifying probiotic enzymes implicated in essential metabolic pathways is highly relevant to the development of future strategies targeting dysbiosis and related diseases. Herein, we report the first biochemical characterization of β-class carbonic anhydrase (CA) from Bifidobacterium longum (BloCAβ) by inhibition and activation profiles. The enzyme was recombinantly expressed, purified, and kinetically characterized, displaying a catalytic efficiency within the same order of magnitude as, although lower than, that of human (h)CA I. The functional profile of this novel CA was explored using a panel of commercial sulfonamides, sulfamides, sulfamates, and inorganic/organic anions as inhibitors. Furthermore, several biogenic amines and amino acids were assessed as potential activators of BloCAβ, and their activation profiles were compared with those of hCAs I and II. The cellular effects of selected BloCAβ activators was further evaluated in human macrophages under basal and proinflammatory conditions, while the safety profile was assessed in human intestinal epithelial cells (HIECs). Among them, serotonin (38) was found to significantly enhance cell metabolic activity in both conditions and preserve the metabolic activity of HIECs, further supporting its biocompatibility. Overall, these results provide the first biochemical and functional characterization of BloCAβ and establish a biochemical basis for future studies investigating the physiological role of probiotic CAs in bacterial models.

rows.title: Preventive effect of goshajinkigan on paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy: an open-label, randomized phase II study (OLCSG2101).
rows.verified_title: Preventive effect of goshajinkigan on paclitaxel-induced peripheral neuropathy: an open-label, randomized phase II study (OLCSG2101).
rows.focus: Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) is a dose-limiting toxicity of paclitaxel (PTX)-containing regimens, and no preventive strategy has been established. We evaluated goshajinkigan (GJG), a traditional Japanese herbal medicine (Kampo), for preventing CIPN during PTX-containing chemotherapy. In this open-label, randomized phase II trial across 7 institutions in Japan, patients with malignant tumors scheduled for ≥4 courses of carboplatin plus PTX (≥150 mg/m²) were randomized 1:1 to GJG or control, with minimization by cancer type and age. The primary endpoint was grade ≥2 CIPN incidence within 4 courses. The protocol-prespecified primary analysis used an unstratified 2-sided log-rank test (α = 0.10); a supportive stratified analysis accounted for the minimization factors. Sixty-five patients were randomized (GJG, 32; control, 33); 52 (80.0%) had lung cancer. Grade ≥2 CIPN occurred in 28.1% (9/32) of the GJG arm vs 51.5% (17/33) of the control arm; the protocol-prespecified unstratified log-rank P value was .013, with a corresponding HR of 0.34 (90% CI, 0.16-0.72). In the stratified analysis accounting for cancer type and age, the estimate remained in favor of GJG but was attenuated and less precise (HR, 0.48; 90% CI, 0.22-1.02; stratified log-rank P = .101). Grade 3-5 adverse-event incidence was similar between arms. GJG was associated with fewer grade ≥2 CIPN events in this predominantly lung-cancer population. Given the open-label design and uncertainty in the stratified analysis, these findings represent a phase II preventive signal warranting confirmation in a double-blind, placebo-controlled phase III trial. Japan Registry of Clinical Trials (jRCTs061210047).
